title: Epiretinal Membrane: Comprehensive Clinical Guide
summary: A deep dive into the pathophysiology, OCT-based staging, and surgical management of Epiretinal Membranes (ERM), ranging from subtle cellophane maculopathy to vision-threatening macular pucker. This guide integrates classic Gass classification with modern Govetto staging and surgical protocols.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Epiretinal Membrane (ERM) is a common vitreoretinal condition characterized by the proliferation of a fibrocellular tissue on the inner surface of the internal limiting membrane (ILM). Clinically, it ranges from an asymptomatic 'cellophane maculopathy' to a 'macular pucker' causing significant metamorphopsia and central vision loss.

rows: Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD) - found in 75-90% of cases, Age (>50).
Retinal Detachment repair (highest risk), Cryopexy, Laser Photocoagulation.
Diabetic Retinopathy, Retinal Vein Occlusion (RVO), Macroaneurysms.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Cellular Mechanism
content: Step 1: PVD induces micro-breaks or dehiscence in the Internal Limiting Membrane (ILM).
Step 2: Migration of glial cells (astrocytes, Müller cells) and RPE cells (if retinal breaks present) through ILM holes.
Step 3: Proliferation of these cells on the retinal surface forming a collagenous membrane.
Step 4: Transdifferentiation of cells into myofibroblasts containing alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA).
Step 5: Centripetal contraction of the membrane leading to retinal folding, vascular tortuosity, and edema.

branches: Stage 2: Macular Pucker (opaque, severe distortion, edema/hemorrhage)

rows: Foveal depression present; well-defined retinal layers.
Loss of foveal depression; all retinal layers identifiable.
Ectopic Inner Retinal Layers (EIRL) present; all layers identifiable.
EIRL present; significant distortion/disorganization of retinal layers.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Metamorphopsia (Amsler Grid distortion)
Micropsia (objects appear smaller) or Macropsia
Decreased Central Visual Acuity (gradual)
Monocular Diplopia (rare)
Difficulty reading despite updated refraction

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Sliver/Cellophane sheen on the macula
Straightening or tortuosity of retinal vessels
Retinal striae (wrinkling)
Pseudohole (centripetal displacement of foveal edges)
Small retinal hemorrhages or exudates (severe cases)
Cotton wool spots (secondary to tractional ischemia)

rows: Watzke-Allen positive, complete neurosensory defect on OCT.
Schisis of outer/inner retina, 'anvil' or 'mustache' shape on OCT.
Normal central foveal thickness, steepened foveal pits, no tissue loss.
Vitreous attachment visible on OCT pulling the foveal contour.
Intraretinal cysts without a visible surface membrane.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. BCVA and Amsler Grid Testing
2. Dilated Fundus Exam (90D or Contact Lens)
3. SD-OCT or SS-OCT (Crucial for staging)
4. Fluorescein Angiography (if vascular leakage/CME suspected)
5. Microperimetry (to assess functional loss in Stage 3/4)

sections.title: Surgical Steps: PPV + Membrane Peel
content: 1. 23G, 25G, or 27G Pars Plana Vitrectomy
2. Induction of PVD (if not already present)
3. Chromovitrectomy (Staining with Brilliant Blue or ICG)
4. Initiation of ERM 'flap' using Tano scraper or end-gripping forceps
5. Centripetal peeling of ERM and ILM (Double peeling or En-bloc)
6. Peripheral retinal inspection for breaks

rows: Low toxicity, excellent contrast, no light sensitivity issues.
Excellent staining, potential RPE toxicity if high concentration/long dwell.
Helps visualize vitreous and ERM edge; doesn't stain ILM.
Good for dense ERM, does not stain ILM well.

sections.title: Red Flags & Contraindications
content: Rapid vision loss (suggests RD or CNV, not just ERM)
Uncontrolled Glaucoma (risk of IOP spikes post-op)
Active Intraocular Inflammation
Presence of significant Outer Retinal Atrophy (EZ loss indicates poor prognosis)
Patient unable to comply with post-op care/positioning

content.explanation: P: PVD (Primary cause); U: Uveitis (Secondary cause); C: Cellophane sheen; K: Keratometry/Refraction change; E: Ectopic Inner Retinal Layers (OCT); R: Retinal striae; S: Surgery (PPV + Peel).

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Post-operative Cataract (nearly 100% within 2 years in phakic patients)
Retinal Detachment (1-2%)
Endophthalmitis (<0.1%)
Scotoma (secondary to ILM peeling or forceps trauma)
Dissociated Optic Nerve Fiber Layer (DONFL) - asymptomatic pits on OCT
Recurrence (rare, <5% with ILM peeling)

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: ILM peeling significantly reduces the rate of ERM recurrence.
Ectopic Inner Retinal Layers (EIRL) thickness is the strongest predictor of final visual acuity.
Wait at least 6-12 months for maximal visual recovery post-peel.
Binocularity is often improved after surgery even if Snellen acuity gain is modest.
Always warn phakic patients that they WILL need cataract surgery.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: Inverted ILM Flap Technique: Being explored for ERM associated with large lamellar holes.
Robot-Assisted Peeling: Emerging technology to reduce tremor and increase precision.
Intraoperative OCT (iOCT): Real-time visualization of the peeling plane and residual traction.
Govetto et al. (2017): Established the importance of EIRL in ERM prognosis.
ERM with Foveoschisis: Surgery should be considered earlier as outcomes are worse once outer retinal damage occurs.
